---
title: "How do you catch the moment a process changed?"
subtitle: "No single measurement gives the shift away, so you keep a running score and wait for the evidence to pile up."
engine: knitr
---

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="cusum-figure" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · one hundred measurements of a process that should average 10 · made-up data"}
:::

A factory makes bolts that should be exactly 10 cm long. Every hour you measure one. The measurements bounce around a little, which is normal random variation. At some point the machine drifts and starts making bolts that are slightly too long, and you want to know when.

You cannot answer by looking at one measurement, because any single value might be high by chance. In the figure the mean does move partway through, by about as much as the noise itself, and each point still looks reasonable on its own. You need a method that accumulates evidence over time and speaks up only when it is confident. That method is CUSUM, short for **cu**mulative **sum**.

## A running score

The idea is to keep a score. Start it at zero. At each time step, ask whether the new observation is above what you expect. If it is, add to the score. If it is not, subtract from it, but never let it go below zero. When the score crosses a threshold, declare a change.

It works like a detective building a case. One above-average observation is a small piece of evidence and convinces nobody. When the pieces keep arriving, the case eventually closes.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="cusum-figure" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · the same measurements, and the score computed from them · made-up data"}
:::

You might try the plain cumulative sum of the deviations from the mean. It shows the trend, but it is noisy before the shift, because random below-average values drag it down. CUSUM adds two things to fix that, an allowance and a floor at zero:

$$S_t = \max(0, \; S_{t-1} + (x_t - \mu) - C)$$

and you declare a change when $S_t > T$. That is the whole method.

| Symbol | What it is | Plain English |
|:------:|:-----------|:-------------|
| $S_t$ | CUSUM statistic at time $t$ | The running score (accumulated evidence) |
| $S_{t-1}$ | Previous score | What we had so far |
| $x_t$ | Current observation | The new measurement |
| $\mu$ | Expected mean | What the process *should* be producing |
| $x_t - \mu$ | Deviation | How far this observation is from expected |
| $C$ | Allowance (critical value) | Filters out normal noise, so only "big enough" deviations count |
| $\max(0, \dots)$ | Floor at zero | Prevents negative accumulation, so past good behavior doesn't mask future problems |
| $T$ | Threshold | How much evidence you need before declaring a change |

Read as a procedure, each time step goes like this. Take the new observation $x_t$. Compute its deviation $x_t - \mu$. Subtract the allowance $C$, which discards small, normal fluctuations. Add the result to the previous score $S_{t-1}$. If the total is negative, reset it to 0. If $S_t > T$, sound the alarm.

In Fig. 2 the mean moves up by 0.3 cm after $t = 60$, with noise of the same size. With $C = 0.15$ and $T = 2$ the score stays near zero while nothing is wrong, starts climbing right after the change, and crosses the threshold at $t = 72$. The twelve steps in between are the detection delay.

## Two knobs

$C$ is a filter. It is subtracted from every deviation, so that ordinary fluctuations do not accumulate. With a large $C$, only big deviations count: detection is slower and false alarms are fewer. With a small $C$, small deviations count too: detection is faster and false alarms are more frequent. At $C = 0$ every above-average observation adds to the score, which makes it very sensitive.

$T$ sets how certain you need to be before declaring a change. A large $T$ asks for a lot of evidence, which gives fewer false alarms and slower detection. A small $T$ triggers on less evidence, which gives faster detection and more false alarms.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="cusum-figure" data-step="2" data-steps="2:slide C and T|3:change the shift" data-caption="Fig. 3 · computed live in your browser; the score restarts after each false alarm · made-up data"}
:::

Both knobs therefore turn the same way, and this is the central tradeoff of the method. Small $C$ and small $T$ give fast detection and more false alarms. Large $C$ and large $T$ give slow detection and fewer false alarms. You cannot have both. In Fig. 3, set $C$ to zero and the alarm comes at $t = 64$ instead of 72, at the price of a false alarm early on. Push $C$ to 0.4 and the score never reaches the threshold at all: no false alarms, and no detection either. [Exam trap: "What happens if we increase T?" Fewer false alarms, slower detection. "What happens if we increase C?" The same effect. Neither has a universal best value.]{.side}

The right values depend on what each kind of mistake costs.

| Scenario | Want | Set |
|:---------|:-----|:----|
| Nuclear reactor monitoring | Fast detection (safety!) | Small C, small T |
| Marketing campaign tracking | Few false alarms (budget!) | Large C, large T |
| Manufacturing quality | Balance both | Moderate C and T |

The second button under Fig. 3 changes the size of the shift itself. A small, persistent shift is exactly what CUSUM is for, but the smaller it is, the longer the evidence takes to pile up.

## The floor, and the other direction

The $\max(0, \dots)$ is not decoration. Without it, a long stretch of below-average values would build up a large negative score. When a real shift then happens, the score has to climb back out of that hole before it can trigger an alarm, and detection is late. The proper CUSUM resets to zero whenever it would go negative, so every moment is a potential fresh start for detecting a change.

The formula so far only detects increases. To detect decreases, run a second score with the deviation mirrored:

$$S_t^+ = \max(0, \; S_{t-1}^+ + (x_t - \mu) - C) \quad \text{(detects increase)}$$

$$S_t^- = \max(0, \; S_{t-1}^- - (x_t - \mu) - C) \quad \text{(detects decrease)}$$

and raise the alarm when either $S_t^+ > T$ or $S_t^- > T$. This is the two-sided CUSUM.

## What an alarm tells you

CUSUM tells you **when** something changed. It does not tell you what changed or why. Suppose it detects a shift in manufacturing quality at day 60. "The machine is broken" is the wrong conclusion. The right one is "something changed around day 60, and we need to investigate what happened." CUSUM is a detection tool, not a diagnosis tool, and the investigation happens after the alarm. [Exam trap: an alarm is a time, not a cause. CUSUM detects; it does not diagnose.]{.side}

The same score works wherever a measurement arrives in sequence and has an expected level.

| Application | What $x_t$ measures | What "change" means |
|:------------|:-------------------|:-------------------|
| Manufacturing | Part dimension | Machine needs recalibration |
| Healthcare | Patient vitals | Condition is deteriorating |
| Finance | Transaction amounts | Potential fraud pattern |
| Website | Page load times | Server performance degraded |
| Retail | Daily sales | Market shift or competitor action |

It also helps to know what CUSUM is not.

| Method | Detects | When to use |
|:-------|:--------|:------------|
| **CUSUM** | Shift in process mean | Ongoing monitoring, small persistent shifts |
| **Control chart** | Individual outlier points | Quick spikes, obvious violations |
| **t-test** | Difference between two groups | Comparing before/after with known breakpoint |
| **Exponential smoothing** | Trends and patterns | Forecasting future values |

Its strength is the small, gradual shift that individual observations cannot reveal. A single point might look normal, but CUSUM accumulates the evidence until the pattern is undeniable.

## Run it yourself {.reference}

Every plot below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

A process with mean 10 that shifts by 0.5 at $t = 60$, with 0.3 of natural variation.

```{r}
#| label: plot-the-problem
#| fig-cap: "Can you spot where the process shifted? It's hard to tell from individual points."

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

# Normal process, then a shift at t = 60
n <- 100
mu <- 10       # expected mean
shift <- 0.5   # how much the mean shifts

x <- c(rnorm(60, mu, 0.3), rnorm(40, mu + shift, 0.3))
time <- 1:n

df <- data.frame(time = time, value = x)

ggplot(df, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_point(color = "gray40", size = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mu, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = mu + 0.15, label = "Expected mean (μ = 10)",
           color = "steelblue", size = 3.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, color = "coral", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 63, y = 9.2, label = "True shift\n(unknown to us)",
           color = "coral", size = 3.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Measurement (cm)",
       title = "Individual measurements — the shift is buried in noise")
```

The individual deviations from $\mu$, and their naive cumulative sum.

```{r}
#| label: plot-accumulation
#| fig-cap: "CUSUM accumulates positive deviations. When they pile up, a change is detected."

# Simple visual: show deviations accumulating
deviations <- x - mu

colors <- ifelse(deviations > 0, "coral", "steelblue")

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(3, 4, 3, 1))

# Top: individual deviations
barplot(deviations, col = adjustcolor(colors, 0.6), border = NA,
  main = "Individual deviations from μ (each observation - 10)",
  ylab = "Deviation", names.arg = rep("", n))
abline(h = 0)
mtext("After the shift, more bars are positive (red)", side = 1, line = 1, cex = 0.8)

# Bottom: cumulative sum
cumdev <- cumsum(deviations)
plot(time, cumdev, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
  main = "Naive cumulative sum of deviations",
  ylab = "Cumulative Sum", xlab = "Time")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
abline(v = 60, col = "coral", lty = 3)
text(65, max(cumdev) * 0.3, "Shift here →", col = "coral", cex = 0.9)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The CUSUM statistic with $C = 0.2$ and $T = 4$, and the time it first crosses the threshold.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cusum-formula
#| fig-cap: "CUSUM in action: the score accumulates after the shift and crosses the threshold"

# Compute CUSUM
C_val <- 0.2  # allowance
T_val <- 4    # threshold

S <- numeric(n)
S[1] <- max(0, (x[1] - mu) - C_val)

for (t in 2:n) {
  S[t] <- max(0, S[t - 1] + (x[t] - mu) - C_val)
}

# When does it cross T?
alarm_time <- which(S > T_val)[1]

df_cusum <- data.frame(time = time, S = S)

ggplot(df_cusum, aes(time, S)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = T_val, color = "coral", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 15, y = T_val + 0.5,
           label = paste0("Threshold T = ", T_val), color = "coral", size = 4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, color = "gray50", linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 55, y = max(S) * 0.8, label = "True shift", color = "gray50", size = 3.5) +
  { if (!is.na(alarm_time))
    list(
      geom_vline(xintercept = alarm_time, color = "darkred", linewidth = 1),
      annotate("text", x = alarm_time + 3, y = T_val + 1.5,
               label = paste0("ALARM at t = ", alarm_time),
               color = "darkred", fontface = "bold", size = 4)
    )
  } +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = expression(S[t] ~ "(CUSUM statistic)"),
       title = "CUSUM detects the shift")
```

The same data at three values of $C$.

```{r}
#| label: plot-c-effect
#| fig-cap: "Larger C = slower detection but fewer false alarms"

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (C_test in c(0.05, 0.2, 0.5)) {
  S_test <- numeric(n)
  S_test[1] <- max(0, (x[1] - mu) - C_test)
  for (t in 2:n) {
    S_test[t] <- max(0, S_test[t - 1] + (x[t] - mu) - C_test)
  }

  alarm <- which(S_test > T_val)[1]

  plot(time, S_test, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
    main = paste0("C = ", C_test),
    xlab = "Time", ylab = expression(S[t]),
    ylim = c(0, max(S_test, T_val + 1)))
  abline(h = T_val, col = "coral", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  abline(v = 60, col = "gray50", lty = 3)

  if (!is.na(alarm)) {
    abline(v = alarm, col = "darkred", lwd = 1.5)
    legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
      legend = c(
        paste0("Alarm at t = ", alarm),
        paste0("Delay: ", alarm - 60, " steps")
      ))
  } else {
    legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, legend = "No alarm triggered")
  }
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The same score against three values of $T$.

```{r}
#| label: plot-t-effect
#| fig-cap: "Larger T = more evidence needed before triggering an alarm"

# Fix C, vary T
C_fixed <- 0.2

S_fixed <- numeric(n)
S_fixed[1] <- max(0, (x[1] - mu) - C_fixed)
for (t in 2:n) {
  S_fixed[t] <- max(0, S_fixed[t - 1] + (x[t] - mu) - C_fixed)
}

T_vals <- c(2, 4, 8)
alarm_times <- sapply(T_vals, function(Tv) which(S_fixed > Tv)[1])

df_t <- data.frame(time = time, S = S_fixed)

ggplot(df_t, aes(time, S)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = T_vals[1], color = "coral", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = T_vals[2], color = "darkorange", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = T_vals[3], color = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = T_vals[1] + 0.4,
           label = paste0("T=2 → alarm at t=", alarm_times[1]), color = "coral", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = T_vals[2] + 0.4,
           label = paste0("T=4 → alarm at t=", alarm_times[2]), color = "darkorange", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = T_vals[3] + 0.4,
           label = paste0("T=8 → alarm at t=",
                          ifelse(is.na(alarm_times[3]), "never", alarm_times[3])),
           color = "darkred", size = 3.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, color = "gray50", linetype = "dotted") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = expression(S[t]),
       title = "Same data, different thresholds")
```

The score with and without the floor at zero.

```{r}
#| label: plot-max-zero
#| fig-cap: "Without max(0,...), past good behavior delays detection of real changes"

C_demo <- 0.2

# With max(0, ...)
S_with <- numeric(n)
S_with[1] <- max(0, (x[1] - mu) - C_demo)
for (t in 2:n) {
  S_with[t] <- max(0, S_with[t - 1] + (x[t] - mu) - C_demo)
}

# Without max(0, ...) — naive version
S_without <- numeric(n)
S_without[1] <- (x[1] - mu) - C_demo
for (t in 2:n) {
  S_without[t] <- S_without[t - 1] + (x[t] - mu) - C_demo
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

plot(time, S_with, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
  main = "With max(0,...)",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = expression(S[t]))
abline(h = T_val, col = "coral", lty = 2)
abline(v = 60, col = "gray50", lty = 3)
alarm1 <- which(S_with > T_val)[1]
if (!is.na(alarm1)) {
  abline(v = alarm1, col = "darkred")
  text(alarm1 + 3, T_val + 1, paste("t =", alarm1), col = "darkred", cex = 0.9)
}

plot(time, S_without, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
  main = "Without max(0,...)",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = expression(S[t]))
abline(h = T_val, col = "coral", lty = 2)
abline(v = 60, col = "gray50", lty = 3)
alarm2 <- which(S_without > T_val)[1]
if (!is.na(alarm2)) {
  abline(v = alarm2, col = "darkred")
  text(alarm2 + 3, T_val + 1, paste("t =", alarm2), col = "darkred", cex = 0.9)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

A process that shifts down at $t = 50$, monitored with both scores.

```{r}
#| label: plot-two-sided
#| fig-cap: "Two-sided CUSUM catches both upward and downward shifts"

set.seed(99)

# Process with a DECREASE at t=50
x2 <- c(rnorm(50, 10, 0.3), rnorm(50, 9.4, 0.3))

S_up <- numeric(n)
S_down <- numeric(n)
C2 <- 0.2

for (t in 2:n) {
  S_up[t] <- max(0, S_up[t - 1] + (x2[t] - mu) - C2)
  S_down[t] <- max(0, S_down[t - 1] - (x2[t] - mu) - C2)
}

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(3, 4, 3, 1))

plot(time, x2, pch = 19, cex = 0.8, col = "gray40",
  main = "Data with a DECREASE at t = 50",
  ylab = "Value", xlab = "")
abline(h = mu, col = "steelblue", lty = 2)
abline(v = 50, col = "gray50", lty = 3)

plot(time, S_up, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "coral",
  ylim = c(0, max(c(S_up, S_down, T_val + 1))),
  main = "Two-sided CUSUM", ylab = expression(S[t]), xlab = "Time")
lines(time, S_down, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = T_val, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
legend("topleft", bty = "n",
  legend = c("S⁺ (detects increase)", "S⁻ (detects decrease)", "Threshold"),
  col = c("coral", "steelblue", "gray40"), lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = 2, cex = 0.8)

alarm_down <- which(S_down > T_val)[1]
if (!is.na(alarm_down)) {
  abline(v = alarm_down, col = "darkred")
  text(alarm_down + 3, T_val + 0.5, paste("Alarm t =", alarm_down),
       col = "darkred", cex = 0.9)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

CUSUM on website response times that degrade after day 50.

```{r}
#| label: plot-real-world
#| fig-cap: "CUSUM applied to website response times — detects server degradation"

set.seed(42)

# Website response time (ms)
days <- 1:90
resp_time <- c(
  rnorm(50, 200, 20),   # normal
  rnorm(40, 230, 25)    # degraded after day 50
)

mu_web <- 200
C_web <- 5
T_web <- 80

S_web <- numeric(90)
for (t in 2:90) {
  S_web[t] <- max(0, S_web[t - 1] + (resp_time[t] - mu_web) - C_web)
}

alarm_web <- which(S_web > T_web)[1]

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(3, 4, 3, 1))

plot(days, resp_time, pch = 19, cex = 0.8, col = "gray40",
  main = "Website Response Time (ms)",
  ylab = "Response Time", xlab = "")
abline(h = mu_web, col = "steelblue", lty = 2)

plot(days, S_web, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
  main = "CUSUM Monitoring", ylab = expression(S[t]), xlab = "Day")
abline(h = T_web, col = "coral", lty = 2)
if (!is.na(alarm_web)) {
  abline(v = alarm_web, col = "darkred")
  text(alarm_web + 3, T_web + 10,
    paste0("Alert: investigate server\n(day ", alarm_web, ")"),
    col = "darkred", cex = 0.8)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## On one page {.reference}

```
THE CUSUM RECIPE
=================

1. PURPOSE: Detect when a process mean has shifted

2. THE FORMULA:
   Sₜ = max(0, Sₜ₋₁ + (xₜ - μ) - C)

   Alarm when Sₜ > T

3. SYMBOLS:
   Sₜ  = accumulated evidence (running score)
   xₜ  = current observation
   μ   = expected baseline mean
   C   = allowance (noise filter)
   T   = threshold (alarm trigger)

4. KEY PARAMETERS:
   C → how much noise to ignore
   T → how much evidence needed for alarm
   Both: ↑ value = slower detection, fewer false alarms
         ↓ value = faster detection, more false alarms

5. WHY max(0,...)?
   Prevents past good behavior from masking future changes.
   Every moment is a fresh start for detection.

6. TWO-SIDED:
   S⁺ detects increases, S⁻ detects decreases

7. CUSUM CANNOT:
   - Tell you WHY something changed
   - Tell you WHAT changed
   - Only tells you WHEN

8. COMMON PITFALLS:
   - No universal best C and T (depends on costs)
   - "Increase T" → fewer false alarms, slower detection
   - CUSUM detects, it doesn't diagnose
```

## Check yourself {.reference}

Before moving on, try to answer these without scrolling up:

1. What does CUSUM stand for and what does it detect?
2. Walk through the formula $S_t = \max(0, S_{t-1} + (x_t - \mu) - C)$
   in plain English.
3. What does $C$ (allowance) control? What happens if you increase it?
4. What does $T$ (threshold) control? What happens if you decrease it?
5. Why is the $\max(0, \dots)$ necessary? What would happen without it?
6. CUSUM triggers an alarm. Can you conclude the machine is broken? Why
   or why not?
7. A nuclear power plant wants fast detection at all costs. A marketing
   team wants to avoid false alarms. How should each set C and T?
8. How is CUSUM different from just looking at individual measurements?
